documents: Rowley & Forte (2022), JGR Solid Earth 127, e2020JB021638, published paper (PDF, 24 pages); no supplement, review file or earlier version supplied
pages_convention: printed journal pages (n of 24), identical to PDF pages counted from 1

entry.evidence: In the analysis presented in the main text, we focus on the hypothesis that slab-pull torques are the primary drivers of observed plate motions

steps.action: The authors recall their earlier reconstruction of persistent asymmetric spreading, long ridge residence times and limited ridge-perpendicular motion of the EPR.
steps.quote: Rowley et al. (2016) highlighted that the EPR is characterized by persistent anomalous asymmetry in spreading.

steps.action: They state the community hypothesis that slab-pull and ridge-push drive plates, with mid-ocean ridges as passive boundaries that migrate ridge-perpendicular.
steps.quote: Plate tectonics has long been considered to be largely driven by slab-pull

steps.action: They state the rival from their earlier work: deep-mantle upwelling beneath the EPR exerts basal tractions that drive the Pacific and Farallon/Nazca plates (about 50%).
steps.quote: A major conclusion of their study is that mantle-convection-driven basal shear stresses acting below tectonic plates is a major contributor to plate motions

steps.action: They pose the question whether subduction-related torques, rather than the earlier buoyancy-flux proxy, can account for the EPR's observed lack of ridge-perpendicular motion.
steps.quote: The buoyancy flux proxy of Rowley et al. (2016) thus needs to be converted to the corresponding torques

steps.action: They derive the slab-pull force, the slab-pull, transform-resistance, collision-resistance and viscous-drag torques, and the zero-net-torque balance that gives each plate's rotation vector in the NNR frame (Equations 1-8, Appendix A).
steps.quote: the sum of all torques acting on each tectonic plate must be zero

steps.action: They design eight model scenarios that vary slab-pull reduction factors, collision and transform resistance and drag coefficients (Table 1). Trench ages and lengths come from the Müller et al. (2008) paleo-age grids and the Gurnis et al. (2012) polygons, and transform segments are identified algorithmically.
steps.quote: we explore eight models incorporating slab-pull with various estimates of the resistive forces

steps.action: For models 1-7 they estimate the drag coefficient D by fitting the 5 Ma Nazca-Pacific rotation, and they report the implied asthenosphere depth and viscosity. Model 8 uses an a-priori D.
steps.quote: These optimized drag coefficients along with their corresponding depth of deformation and viscosity values are summarized in Table 1.

steps.action: They build the observed/kinematic comparison set of Pacific and Nazca isochrons from the age grid and published rotations, assuming 44/56% spreading asymmetry back to 80 Ma.
steps.quote: as the observed/model data that we use as our comparison set

steps.action: They integrate the torque-derived rotations to retrodict synthetic Farallon/Pacific isochrons for each model by two approaches: half-angle about a template near the EPR, and full rotation with the Pacific fixed (Figures 1, 3).
steps.quote: Figure 2 shows the two approaches that we use to reconstruct synthetic isochrons along this segment of the EPR.

steps.action: They compare predicted and observed oceanic ages at six Peru-Chile Trench sites (Table 2) and quantify the percent error.
steps.quote: For the oldest oceanic lithosphere in the Peru-Chile trench the age differences are generally >5 million years.

steps.action: They compare gridded age distributions using overlap, correlation coefficients and percent error (Table 3, GMT surface gridding) and find poor fits for all models.
steps.quote: Based on Table 3 none of the models yield what would be generally considered a good fit to the data.

steps.action: They examine the best-fitting models 4 and 7 and show that their fit needs plate-specific slab pull and order-of-magnitude contrasts in D that are physically unjustified.
steps.quote: this fit is achieved through extreme variability of the physical input parameters

steps.action: They compare torque-retrodicted EPR positions at 5 Myr intervals back to 80 Ma (Figures 4, 5) with the northward EPR trajectory from global kinematics.
steps.quote: the majority of the torque-derived models retrodict a west to east migration of the EPR with time.

steps.action: They extend the kinematic comparison to 80 Ma in the Indo-Atlantic hotspot frame and check that it agrees with the NNR frame.
steps.quote: The first order kinematics of the EPR in the NNR and Indo-Atlantic frames of reference are not significantly different.

steps.action: They reject slab-pull plus boundary-resistance torques as the explanation of EPR kinematics, because the retrodicted motions are orthogonal to the observed motions and the age distributions misfit.
steps.quote: most of the torque-derived models yield reconstructed motions of the EPR that are effectively orthogonal and hence incompatible to the observed kinematics

steps.action: They argue that paleo-age-grid uncertainty cannot explain the discrepancy, since it persists at recent ages, and they test laterally varying drag coefficients, which change rotation rates but not the pole positions.
steps.quote: we carried out simulations in which the drag coefficients under each plate differ, by as much as an order of magnitude

steps.action: They compute present-day Pacific plate motions predicted by mantle flow driven by the V1 joint tomography density model (Lu et al., 2020) for three buoyancy cases.
steps.quote: explicitly demonstrate the geodynamic importance of this deep-seated positive buoyancy

steps.action: They compare the full-buoyancy prediction with observed GEODVEL plate velocities and find an excellent rms fit (Figure 6a,b).
steps.quote: characterized by a global root-mean-square (rms) velocity difference of only 0.25 cm/yr relative to the observed global rms velocity of 4.38 cm/yr

steps.action: They remove the deep EPR buoyancy, or keep only it (Figure 6c,d), and quantify the resulting reductions and contributions to Pacific and Nazca plate velocities and the asymmetry of the flow.
steps.quote: Figure 6c shows the predicted plate motions, when all positive buoyancy below the EPR is removed for all depths greater than 400 km.

steps.action: They estimate the basal-traction torques from the deep EPR buoyancy (6.0 and 2.0 × 10^26 N m) and compare them with net slab-pull torques (5.2 and 1.6 × 10^26 N m).
steps.quote: we find that the torque due to the basal tractions on the Pacific and Nazca plates exerted by deep positive buoyancy below the EPR

steps.action: They keep the claim that deep-mantle buoyancy beneath the EPR controls EPR evolution and contributes about as much as slab pull to Pacific plate motions.
steps.quote: deep mantle buoyancy, along with slab-pull related negative buoyancy, jointly provide the primary contributors to plate motions.

tree.answer: EPR fixed in longitude, migrating S to N, with persistent asymmetric spreading
No; reconstructed from magnetic anomalies, age grids and plate rotations
Test whether slab-pull and resistive torques explain EPR kinematics
Slab-pull-dominated passive ridge versus deep-mantle basal tractions
Slab-pull torques predict W-E EPR migration; kinematics show S-N
Found: past plate configurations from paleo-age grids, 80 Ma to present
Misfit survives eight parameter sets, two isochron approaches, two reference frames and variable D
Slab-pull alone excluded; basal tractions best explanation

end.claim: Slab-pull and boundary-resistance torques cannot reproduce the EPR's age distributions or its south-to-north motion since 80 Ma. Basal tractions from deep-mantle buoyancy beneath the EPR best explain EPR kinematics and contribute roughly as much as slab pull to Pacific plate motions.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing torque-retrodicted EPR trajectories with global kinematic reconstructions showed the two are orthogonal (eastward versus northward); without this comparison there is no exclusion of slab-pull control.

gates.evidence: The slab-pull hypothesis directed which torques were computed and compared (p. 22), but all data were pre-existing published age grids and rotations. The slab-pull models could have matched the observed EPR motion and age distributions, and the V1 flow model could have failed to match GEODVEL velocities. Nothing was fixed in advance: D was optimized against recent plate motions, and the authors call the result 'intuitively obvious' beforehand (p. 3) without any registration.

imports.item: Couette shear flow as the model for viscous basal drag
moment-of-inertia-like tensor and Euler's theorem for rigid rotations on a sphere
infinite Prandtl number (negligible inertia) and high Peclet number assumptions
continuous-curvature splines in tension (GMT surface) for gridding isochrons

novelty_claims.quote: We will thus present a new assessment of subduction-related torques as a function of time

limits: Only the published paper was supplied; the supplementary tables and figures (S1-S5, Figures S1-S2) and any review file were not available, so no review sequence is coded. The basal-traction rival is tested only against present-day plate motions (Figure 6). Its fit to the 80 Ma EPR history relies on the authors' earlier work (Rowley et al., 2016), not on new work here. The ~50% contribution and the torque magnitudes (sub-claim, estimate) carry no stated uncertainty, so this sub-claim falls short of estimate_with_resolution. D is a tuned free parameter in models 1-7, which trades off with slab pull. Asymmetric spreading beyond 51 Ma is assumed. There are internal inconsistencies: a correlation maximum of 0.371 is quoted in the text versus 0.340 in Table 3, and the torques are attributed to 'Figure 3d' where Figure 6d is apparently meant (inference). How the eight models were chosen, and whether others were tried and dropped, is not reported. The composition is coded trace_series (inference), because the rivals were not subjected to a single shared crucial test.

disagreements.target: Classic slab-pull-dominated plate driving force view (Forsyth & Uyeda 1975; Richter 1973a; Solomon & Sleep 1974)
disagreements.support: Torque-balance retrodictions over 80 Ma misfit EPR age distributions and give orthogonal EPR motions, while tomography-based flow shows basal tractions comparable to slab pull.
disagreements.quote: [...] the arguments against active mantle tractions, as put forth in these classic treatments of plate driving forces

disagreements.target: Passive mid-ocean ridge view (Elsasser 1971; Parsons & Richter 1980)
disagreements.support: Passive upwelling cannot account for the persistent 44/56% spreading asymmetry, which the deep-upwelling flow model reproduces.
disagreements.quote: if the EPR is assumed a passive ridge, there is no explanation for the observed spreading asymmetry

disagreements.target: Bird et al. (2008) finite-element plate driving force model
disagreements.support: The authors note that the model folds basal tractions on subducting plates into a 'net slab-pull' term and does not identify their source.
disagreements.quote: An important caveat is that their analysis did not explicitly separate basal tractions from net slab-pull in the assessment of subducting plates.

disagreements.target: Stein et al. (1977) ridge migration expectations
disagreements.support: The authors note that spreading asymmetry is included only as a geometric term, with no driving mechanism.
disagreements.quote: also include spreading asymmetry as a potential geometric contributor, but do not address the drivers of any asymmetric spreading.

disagreements.target: Richter Rolls argument that basal tractions cannot drive plates (Richter 1973a, 1977; Richter & Parsons 1975)
disagreements.support: The authors argue that mantle-wide flow beneath the EPR has comparable depth and horizontal scales, which suppresses Richter Rolls.
disagreements.quote: What is often ignored is that when the scale of the large-scale convection is comparable to the length scale of the plates themselves

alternatives_considered.chosen: Approach 1 (template near the EPR at 0.44 of the rotation, then half-angle rotations) and Approach 2 (Pacific fixed, full rotation), both reported
alternatives_considered.reason: Approach 1 distributes misfit to both plates; Approach 2 forces all misfit onto the Farallon plate and embeds the asymmetry

alternatives_considered.chosen: Spreading asymmetry assumed to persist to 80 Ma
alternatives_considered.reason: Places isochrons farther east and decreases misfit for most models (conservative toward slab-pull models)

alternatives_considered.chosen: D optimized to fit 5 Ma Nazca-Pacific motion (models 1-7)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: A-priori D from GIA viscosity and a 300 km layer (model 8)
alternatives_considered.reason: D treated as free variable; model 8 tests the a-priori value

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Range 25%-75% following Stotz et al. (2018), plus no reduction
alternatives_considered.reason: Dissipation by plate bending and mantle stresses reduces transmitted force

alternatives_considered.chosen: Transform resistance C_T = 2 × 10^11 N/m in models 5-8
alternatives_considered.alternatives: C_T = 2 × 10^12 N/m (Becker & O'Connell 2001); intermediate value in model 4
alternatives_considered.reason: Bird et al. (2008) finite-element models imply strongly reduced fault friction

alternatives_considered.chosen: Constant slab penetration depth of 700 km
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Relaxing the simplification in later analyses
alternatives_considered.reason: Maximum slab depths >620 km (Hayes et al., 2018); simplification used by Faccenna et al. (2012)

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Fixed Indo-Atlantic hotspot frame (O'Neill et al., 2005) to 80 Ma
alternatives_considered.reason: NNR reconstruction only extends back to 45 Ma

alternatives_considered.chosen: V1 density model with the Mitrovica & Forte (2004) viscosity profile
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Other viscosity models tested in Lu et al. (2020)
